traits.name: Tilt
traits.now: Your longest losing run was 6 trades in a row, costing ₹11,894.
traits.why: After several losses, frustration takes over decision-making. Each new loss lowers the bar for the next entry, until trading becomes a way to vent rather than a process.
traits.ideal: A daily loss limit and a maximum number of consecutive losses, after which trading stops for the day.

traits.name: End-of-day desperation
traits.now: Trades opened late in the session lost ₹17,204 (29% win rate).
traits.why: Late-session trades are often attempts to fix the day before it ends. The window is short, liquidity changes, and decisions are rushed.
traits.ideal: A cut-off time for new trades, well before the close.

traits.name: The breakeven trap
traits.now: 3 losing positions were closed in several pieces over time instead of all at once.
traits.why: Selling part of a loser feels like action without fully admitting defeat. The remaining piece becomes a lottery ticket on getting back to breakeven, and it is usually the piece that falls furthest.
traits.ideal: When the stop is hit, the whole position goes in one order.

traits.name: Tail risk blindness
traits.now: Just three trades account for 48% of everything you lost.
traits.why: Most trades feel controlled, so risk feels controlled. But the damage is concentrated in a few moments when discipline slipped. Those few trades decide the year, and they are the ones that never get reviewed.
traits.ideal: No single trade can lose more than a fixed cash amount, set before entry. The worst trades get reviewed first.

traits.name: Big bets, bad outcomes
traits.now: Your largest positions lost ₹6,420 with a 38% win rate.
traits.why: Big positions are usually taken when confidence is high, and high confidence often follows recent success or a strong story. Certainty feels like information, but it is just a feeling.
traits.ideal: Larger size is earned by a setup's track record, not by how convinced you feel today.

traits.name: Risk drift
traits.now: Your first half of trades made ₹9,788; the second half lost ₹12,724.
traits.why: Early success often leads to quietly larger risk, looser selection and more trades. The rules that produced the gains erode one small exception at a time.
traits.ideal: The rules that produced good results are written down and reviewed weekly, so they don't drift.

traits.name: Holding through events
traits.now: Trades held overnight lost ₹15,889, while same-day trades made ₹12,953.
traits.why: Overnight positions face news and gaps you cannot react to. If your edge is intraday, holding overnight swaps a skill-based game for a coin flip.
traits.ideal: Overnight risk is taken only by design, sized for a gap against you.

traits.name: Short-term thinking in long trades
traits.now: Positions you carried for days lost ₹15,889, while your quick trades did better.
traits.why: A trade that was meant to be quick becomes a "long-term investment" once it goes red. The story changes to justify not closing it.
traits.ideal: The holding period is set at entry. A short-term trade that fails is closed, not reclassified.

more.name: Rescue holding
more.now: 58% of your losing trades were carried overnight, versus 31% of winners.
more.why: Carrying a loser overnight postpones the decision to the next session, where it is hoped the problem fixes itself. It turns an intraday mistake into a multi-day exposure.
more.ideal: Intraday trades that go wrong are closed intraday. Overnight holds are planned before entry, not decided by the P&L.

more.name: The one-big-loss problem
more.now: Your worst trade lost ₹7,513, about 5 average wins.
more.why: A single large loss usually starts as a normal trade that was never stopped out. Each small move against you felt too small to act on, until the total was too big to accept.
more.ideal: The maximum loss on any trade is about one average win. Anything bigger is treated as a process failure, not bad luck.

more.name: Day-level spirals
more.now: Your worst day (2025-04-13) lost ₹7,418 across 1 trades.
more.why: Bad days rarely start bad. A normal loss is followed by a push to recover, then a bigger push. By the end of the day, one mistake has become several.
more.ideal: A daily loss limit that ends the session. Tomorrow is a fresh start.

more.name: Revenge trading
more.now: Trades taken straight after a loss lost ₹2,993 in total, at a 52% win rate.
more.why: A loss creates an urge to get even immediately. The next trade is chosen to repair the feeling, not because the setup is there. It is the most expensive trade most people take.
more.ideal: After a loss there is a pause (for example 15 minutes) and the next trade must pass the full checklist.

more.name: Emotional bankroll
more.now: You gave back a large share of your peak profit by the end of the period.
more.why: Giving back gains is hard to accept, so trading continues more aggressively to recover the peak. The peak becomes an anchor, and chasing it deepens the drawdown.
more.ideal: A drawdown limit from the peak. Hitting it triggers a reduction in size and a review.

more.name: Process over outcome gap
more.now: Across 52 trades, the average trade loses ₹56.
more.why: Over a large number of trades, luck mostly cancels out. A negative average across many trades is a process problem, not a bad patch.
more.ideal: The process is changed in one specific way, then measured over the next 30–50 trades.

more.name: Frustration spiral
more.now: Losing streaks run long (6 in a row), and trades after losses are negative on average.
more.why: Each loss adds frustration, and frustration lowers the standard for the next trade. The streak continues not because of the market but because of the state of mind.
more.ideal: After a set number of consecutive losses, stop for the day. The market will be there tomorrow.

more.name: Weekday blind spot
more.now: Sunday is your worst day: 7 trades, 29% win rate, −₹7,534.
more.why: Patterns tied to a day of the week are often about you, not the market: energy levels, routines, expiries, or what happened the day before.
more.ideal: Days that consistently lose get smaller size or no trading until the reason is understood.

more.name: Familiarity comfort
more.now: You trade only 3 underlyings and the average trade loses money.
more.why: Sticking to what you know feels safe. But familiarity can turn into autopilot: trading the instrument because it is there, not because it is set up.
more.ideal: Even familiar instruments need a fresh setup each time.

more.name: Drawdown denial
more.now: At the worst point you were ₹16,189 below your peak.
more.why: A deep drawdown is easy to dismiss as temporary. But the depth of a drawdown shows how much risk was really being taken, regardless of where the account ends up.
more.ideal: A maximum drawdown is set in advance. Reaching it means stopping and reassessing.

more.name: Monday overconfidence
more.why: After a weekend of reading and planning, Monday arrives with strong opinions and pent-up energy. Trades are taken to act on those opinions, ready or not.
more.ideal: Monday starts with observation. Weekend views must be confirmed by price before acting.

more.name: Calendar fixation
more.now: Your best weekday (Wednesday) and worst (Sunday) differ by ₹15,570.
more.why: Large differences between days point to routine and mindset rather than market structure. Your best day shows how you trade when conditions suit you.
more.ideal: Recreate the conditions of your best day (preparation, timing, mood) on the others.

net.ideal: Net P&L after costs is the only number that pays. Judge every change to your trading by its effect here.

gross.ideal: Gross P&L should comfortably exceed costs; if it barely does, trade less, not more.

costs.now: Costs were 7% of what your winners made.
costs.ideal: Costs under 15–20% of gross profit. Fewer trades with larger targets get you there.

winrate.ideal: Win rate only matters alongside payoff. 40% with 2:1 winners beats 60% with 1:2.

payoff.now: Average win is 0.94× the average loss.
payoff.ideal: A payoff above 1.5 gives room for a normal win rate to be profitable.

avgwin.ideal: Winners run to a planned target instead of being taken at the first sign of profit.

avgloss.ideal: Losers closed at a pre-set stop, so the average loss is smaller than the average win.

pf.ideal: A profit factor above 1.3 after costs is a sustainable edge.

worst.now: Your worst trade was ₹7,513, about 4.6 average wins.
worst.ideal: The worst trade is no bigger than one or two average wins.

costsPanel.ideal: Every trade expected to make several times its cost.

leaks.ideal: Leaks are fixed one at a time, starting with the most expensive.

curve.now: At the worst point you were ₹16,189 below your peak.
curve.ideal: A steady upward slope with shallow dips; deep drops mean risk per trade is too high.

instrument.ideal: Capital goes to the instrument where your results are best, not where the action is.

afterwinloss.ideal: The trade after a loss looks like any other trade: same size, same checklist.

diagnosis.ideal: A positive average trade after costs, held steady over hundreds of trades.

rules.now: Rules built from your own mistakes.

patterns.ideal: Do more of what works, pause what consistently doesn't.

busyDay.now: Results by how many trades you made that day.

bestU.now: The names that pay you most.
